title: Compact boards, LED arrays and reliable transfer
summary: Configure ESP8266 peripherals, animate a NeoPixel strip, ring or panel, and verify configuration and telemetry after flashing.
body: Windows 0.1.75 and firmware 0.1.57 include these updates. Android 1.0.21 records the corresponding port requirements; its version number does not mean all Windows features are implemented in the APK.

Select a board and supported peripherals

  1. Select the exact board in Configuration before assigning pins. Board labels such as D7 differ from GPIO numbers: on a Wemos D1 mini, D7 is GPIO13, D6 is GPIO12 and the built-in active-low LED is normally GPIO2.
  2. Add a peripheral from the relevant category. Compact targets support an explicit subset of drivers, including LED arrays and basic digital, analog and PWM devices. Unsupported specialized peripherals cannot be enabled merely by selecting a pin.
  3. Read any compatibility dialog when changing boards. Confirm removal of incompatible elements only after reviewing the affected peripherals and Logics. Save a copy before migrating a project.

ESP8266 supply-voltage measurement and external A0 input are mutually exclusive firmware configurations. Chip temperature is not a calibrated supported ESP8266 sensor. Use the available CPU frequency, heap, uptime, reset and network telemetry instead.

Wire a WS2812B array

  1. Connect the array DI to the configured output GPIO, GND to the common ground and its power input to the correct supply. DI means data input. DO is the output for the next array; leave it disconnected when there is no downstream array.
  2. Do not assign DO to a second ESP GPIO. For the tested Wemos ring, DI is D7/GPIO13, DO is disconnected and the count is 32.
  3. Use a supply sized for the LEDs and appropriate signal-level conversion where required by the array. Do not drive LED power through a GPIO.

Choose the shape and startup values

  1. In Configuration, add Control → WS2812 / NeoPixel LED Strip.
  2. Select Strip or Ring and enter the LED count. For Panel, enter rows and columns and choose progressive or serpentine wiring to match the physical array.
  3. Set the default effect, brightness, RGB colour and speed. The diagram reflects the configured layout and count; changing the drawing does not change the physical wiring.
  4. On the updated device, use Save and apply LED array to change the configured array. Adding a new peripheral driver still requires a rebuild.

Supported effects are solid, blink, breathe, chase, rainbow, Color Wipe, Theater Chase, Theater Chase Rainbow, Colorloop and Scan. This is not the entire WLED effect library. Limits are four arrays, with up to 128 LEDs per array on ESP8266/ESP8285, 32 on ESP32-C2, and 256 on other listed ESP32 targets. Refresh scheduling is cooperative, but transmitting LED data takes a bounded synchronous interval.

Start the ring from Logics

  1. Add or reuse On Start inside the automation group.
  2. Add the configured LED array action and connect On Start.Out to its effect action input.
  3. Select rainbow and 20% brightness, or leave unconnected inputs at the configured defaults. Keep existing sampling connections intact.
  4. Start the group, save the project and flash. Check that the saved group is playing after reboot.

The physical acceptance test used a 32-pixel ring on GPIO13 with a 17-node sampling graph. Configuration was acknowledged, the graph ran without a reported error, and the user confirmed the rainbow effect. Other array sizes and electrical arrangements still require their own hardware test.

Regular LEDs and automatic converters

A regular built-in LED supports PWM brightness when the selected pin and driver support it, but cannot display RGB colours. Select the correct active-low polarity. An execution output such as Sampled is not a numeric measurement: use the numeric source directly, or an Event to Number converter with an explicit value. The converter forwards execution and exposes its configured value; connect both outputs when the action must run after that value is updated. Automatic conversion inserts an editable node for supported type pairs, not an arbitrary conversion for every incompatible connection.

Flash, transfer and verify

  1. Disconnect Serial Monitor and Plotter before flashing so they release the port.
  2. Wait for firmware verification and then configuration applied. Flash completion alone does not confirm that the settings and graph were saved.
  3. Open the reported device IP, refresh the browser and verify the peripheral preview, GPIO, count, effect and Logics group.
  4. For serial plots, reconnect at the firmware runtime baud rate and start a graph containing Transfer to Plotter nodes. For network plots, choose the network transport and enter the device IP.

Garbled ESP8266 boot text followed by readable provisioning messages is not, by itself, evidence of the wrong runtime baud rate. Missing acknowledgements can also mean a rejected graph, low memory, a busy port or a restarted device. Read the reported error before retrying. Windows can compare a device settings snapshot after a missing acknowledgement.

Memory, compression and recovery

Compact firmware stores the editor graph in flash and parses only executable fields into runtime memory. The browser reconstructs the visual graph. Web assets use gzip where generated, and only the selected board artwork is included. Firmware size reduction removes unused peripheral artwork before removing unused drivers and dependencies; configured hardware must be retained.

Flash savings do not create additional SRAM. Graph, request, node and connection limits still apply and very large graphs cannot run on every board. Reduce unnecessary nodes or choose a larger target when runtime limits are exceeded. Provisioning stages the incoming graph in flash, releases old runtime data before validation and preserves the previous settings when validation fails.

Firmware 0.1.57 moves NeoPixel refresh and release into the main loop. HTTP status requests no longer call NeoPixel transmission from the ESP8266 network callback, which previously could trigger a yield panic. Busy HTTP requests now return a JSON error and the compact interface retries initial configuration loading.

Timers, alarms, sleep and saved data

Use Delay for a nonblocking gap between actions, Countdown Timer for Start, Reset, Stop and remaining time, and Timer for periodic triggering. Timed feedback loops require a scheduling boundary; immediate event cycles and circular data dependencies remain invalid. See Wire routing and Bezier controls for the worked three-sample loop.

Alarm Clock supports a date/time schedule and selected weekdays using the configured time source. Use an RTC peripheral only on targets with the required driver. Sleep modes and wake pins depend on the selected chip; deep sleep normally restarts execution on wake. A software event cannot wake a powered-down processor without a supported hardware wake source.

Save Data requires supported external storage. The default recording interval is five seconds; put a Sampling Interval between the value source and recording input to change the cadence. Missing folders are created for a specified path. Real-time plots are not persisted without storage. Where history is supported, use the date/time range and Realtime control to switch between recorded and live data. Compact targets do not acquire unsupported storage or sleep drivers merely because the editor contains those nodes.

Animated previews and smooth effects

Windows and the device page animate the configured strip, ring or panel using the same deterministic pixel calculations as firmware. Set the layout, effect, speed, brightness and RGB values, then compare the preview. The preview shows configured defaults; an explicit Logics action can override those values on the device. It is a simulation, not a camera view or measurement of electrical output.

Frames are scheduled every 25 milliseconds. Discrete effects advance no faster than one pixel per frame. After a network stall, animation resumes without jumping across several pixels. Static and off states avoid repeated data transfers. The firmware, Python and JavaScript calculations are compared by automated tests.

Color Wipe and Theater Chase follow the established patterns in Adafruit NeoPixel strandtest. Scan and Colorloop follow the WLED effect descriptions. The implementation uses a cooperative scheduler rather than the blocking delays in demonstration sketches.

Save and apply waits for the device to finish validating and persisting the configuration. A rejected setting leaves the previous configuration in place. HTTP callbacks queue changes for the main loop rather than applying them in the network callback. If the virtual animation is smooth but the physical LEDs flicker, check the supply, common ground, DI connection and data-signal level before increasing brightness.
